lesson.title: Cutting to the Chase: Net Ionic Equations
lesson.summary: A net ionic equation removes the ions that appear unchanged on both sides of a complete ionic equation, leaving only the species that genuinely participate in the chemical change.
lesson.body:
Look closely at the complete ionic equation from the last chapter: Pb2+(aq) + 2 NO3-(aq) + 2 K+(aq) + 2 I-(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2 K+(aq) + 2 NO3-(aq). The potassium ions and the nitrate ions appear on both sides in exactly the same form: same charge, same physical state, same amount. They start the reaction dissolved in water and end the reaction exactly as dissolved as they were before. Nothing happened to them.

A net ionic equation is what remains after you cancel any ion that appears unchanged on both sides, the same way you would cancel a common term from both sides of an algebraic equation. Canceling 2 K+(aq) and 2 NO3-(aq) from both sides of the equation above leaves: Pb2+(aq) + 2 I-(aq) -> PbI2(s). Checking this simplified equation on its own: 1 lead atom on each side, 2 iodine atoms on each side, and for charge, the left side has plus 2 plus 2 times minus 1, which equals 0, while the right side, a neutral solid, is also 0. The equation is still fully balanced after the cancellation, which is exactly what should happen, since canceling identical terms from both sides of a true equation always preserves it.

The net ionic equation is valuable because it captures the actual chemistry, stripped of whatever specific soluble salts happened to be sitting in the reagent bottles. If you had instead mixed aqueous lead(II) acetate, Pb(C2H3O2)2(aq), which is one of the notable soluble lead salts, with aqueous sodium iodide, NaI(aq), instead of lead nitrate and potassium iodide, you would get a different molecular equation and a different complete ionic equation, with sodium and acetate ions as the spectators instead of potassium and nitrate. But the net ionic equation would be identical: Pb2+(aq) + 2 I-(aq) -> PbI2(s). The precipitate does not care which soluble salt supplied the lead ions or the iodide ions, only that both ions were present in solution together.

This is also why net ionic equations are the preferred way to represent precipitation reactions when the identity of the spectator ions is not the point of interest. They isolate the actual driving force of the reaction, in this case the strong attraction between Pb2+ and I- that overcomes the hydration stabilizing them individually in solution.
